Posted March 23, 2005
Analysis by Richard Cowan

My heart goes out to both sides in the Terry Schiavo case. Her parents and her husband are struggling over a truly excruciating question that is the result of medical science getting ahead of medical ethics (which is not very difficult.)

On the other hand, I have only contempt for the politicians, so-called conservatives, who have trampled on the Constitution, the federal principle, and the rule of law generally to play to the politically pious and the media circus.

Writing about Bills of attainder in The Federalist, Number 44, James Madison said, The sober people of America are weary of the fluctuating policy which has directed the public councils. They have seen with regret and indignation that sudden changes and legislative interferences, in cases affecting personal rights, become jobs in the hands of enterprising and influential speculators, and snares to the more-industrious and less-informed part of the community.

It is hard to imagine a better description of the Congress rushing through a law that granted any parent of Theresa Marie Schiavo the standing the legal right to sue in federal court to keep her on life-support. That is not the rule of law, but pandering to the selectively compassionate.

I am not making light of the present tragedy when I say that it would be interesting to see what would happen to Mrs. Schiavo if a neurologist announced that medical cannabis could bring her back to life. (Obviously, my point is purely hypothetical, and there is no reason to think that it could, but had she been administered cannabis when she had her stroke, she might be in much better shape.)
 Dr. Lester Grinspoon Warns About The Pharmaceuticalization of Cannabis, As GW Pharmaceutical Hits All Time High After Deal With Bayer. But Does It Need Prohibition In Order to Succeed?

In any case, I think that we already know the answer to my question. The Supreme Court will be deciding soon on a very real case that involves two other women who are proxies for many more. Angel Raich's doctors say that she needs cannabis to live, but the Bush Administration fought against her right to life all the way to the top court.
See
 We Have Already Won A Lot From The Supreme Court Case, Which Is Good Because That Is Probably All That We Are Going To Get. DEA Changes The Rules on Treating Pain.

Although there is some controversy about whether Mrs. Schiavo's condition is truly irreversible, the immediate question is whether she must be given food and water to keep her alive artificially.

If one argues that she must be given these substances, then how would that any different from arguing that she must be given another substance, perhaps a pharmaceutical, or perhaps cannabis tea through her feeding tube or cannabis vapors through an inhalation device? If someone has the right to be kept alive under her circumstances, then what difference does it make how it is done?

The real-world answer, of course, is that it makes a great deal of difference. She must be kept alive only by methods approved by the federal government. (And these people call themselves conservatives. "??)

The current dispute arose because Mrs. Schiavo did not provide written instructions a living will to make her wishes clear. If she were to regain consciousness and say that she did not think that her life was worth living, the Bush Administration would then oppose her right to kill herself. (They have gone to court to oppose Oregon's assisted-suicide law.) At least they are consistent in that regard.

On the other hand, those who support assisted suicide and oppose medical cannabis are arguing that people should have the right to take something that will kill them, but not something that would keep them alive and/or even make life worth living.
See
 A Four Twenty Joke from The Washington Post Editorial Page. We Have The Right to Die, But Not To Live.

Over the years that I have been involved in the cannabis controversies, nothing has had a greater impact on me than being told, I haven't tried to kill myself since I started using cannabis.

One person whom I did not have the privilege of knowing was the late Biz Ivol, an incredibly brave Scottish MS patient who attempted suicide after being prosecuted for providing fellow sufferers with cannabis candy.
See
 Scottish MS Patient Says She Will Kill Herself When Trial Is Over. But GW Pharmaceutical's Research Proves That Her Death Will Really Be Murder. The Need for A Patients Rights Organization.
and
 Ethical Failure Of Cannabis Prohibition. Tragedy And Farce. Using the Patients To Protect Prohibition. Analysis by Richard Cowan

Her suicide attempt was not successful, but she died last year. I regret that I failed to note her passing at the time, but the British MS Society estimates that there are thousands more like her who are using cannabis illegally while the UK government dithers over approving GW's whole cannabis extract.
See
 Judicial Murder: Quadriplegic Dies In DC Jail. Compassionate Conservatism At Work? Michigan MS Patient May Get Mercy, If It Does Not Threaten Drug War. Three Stories. Infinite Insanity.
and from 1999
 Swiss MS Society Supports Medical Marijuana.
" Cannabis can be an effective alternative for patients that do not respond to ordinary drugs, "
Swiss Specialist Says. -- Association for Cannabis as Medicine Bulletin

Thus, cannabis may sometimes prevent suicide and being deprived of it may lead to suicide, but none of that matters to the therapeutic state.

As for my hypothetical question, I have no doubt that if her doctors said Mrs. Schiavo needed cannabis to live, those who are arguing that her life is sacred would suddenly find that cannabis prohibition is even more sacred. Indeed, they have already made that agonizingly clear.

 Jeb Bush Embraces The Big Lie On Medical Marijuana With Full Frontal Stupidity
